kit.name: ELEGOO UNO R3 Super Starter Kit

identity.manufacturer: unbranded generic board; onboard chip is commonly Toshiba ULN2003APG or a second-source equivalent (e.g. STMicroelectronics ULN2003A, UTC ULN2003G)
identity.manufacturer_part_number: ULN2003APG (chip); the breakout board itself has no board-level MPN, it is a generic unbranded design
identity.package: module, small PCB carrying one 16-pin DIP driver IC

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A small circuit board that acts like a strong relay for weak signals, letting the tiny electrical pulses from an Arduino control a motor that needs far more current than the Arduino can supply directly.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Driving the 28BYJ-48 stepper motor (or other small 4-phase unipolar stepper motors, or other inductive loads like relays and lamps) from a microcontroller.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Inside is a ULN2003 chip containing seven Darlington transistor pairs. Each pair works like a switch: a small current from an Arduino IN pin flips the switch, letting a much bigger current from the external power supply flow through one motor coil at a time in the right sequence.

pinout.name: IN1
pinout.notes: drives motor coil channel 1; connects to an Arduino digital pin
5-12V supply for the motor coils, can be separate from the Arduino's own power
common ground, must be tied to the Arduino's GND even if using a separate supply

pins.pin_1_identification: IN1-IN4 are printed on the board's silkscreen next to a row of 4 header pins, usually beside 4 small LED indicators that flash as each coil activates. The board also has a separate white 5-pin socket (not part of this 6-pin count) that plugs directly into the stepper motor's cable.

electrical.operating_voltage: 5-12V DC on the motor supply (separate from Arduino logic)
electrical.absolute_max_voltage: the onboard chip is rated to 50V collector-emitter (Toshiba ULN2003APG datasheet), but the board's connectors and traces are only intended for the 5-12V motor supplies used with the 28BYJ-48
electrical.typical_current: varies with the attached motor; per-channel draw for the 28BYJ-48 is roughly 0.1A per active coil
electrical.max_current: 500 mA per channel, absolute maximum, per the Toshiba ULN2003APG manufacturer page
electrical.logic_level: 5V input compatible (standard TTL/CMOS-level input threshold for this chip family)

key_specs.driver_ic: ULN2003 family, 7-channel Darlington transistor array (e.g. Toshiba ULN2003APG)
key_specs.indicator_leds: 4, one per active coil channel, confirmed on the RobotPiShop listing
key_specs.motor_connector: 5-pin JST/XH-style socket wired to match the 28BYJ-48 motor's 5-wire pigtail

visual_identification.shape_and_size: small rectangular PCB roughly 3.5 cm by 1.5 cm
visual_identification.color_and_markings: usually a green or blue PCB; the driver chip is a black 16-pin rectangular DIP package printed with a code like 'ULN2003' or 'ULN2003AN'; four small LEDs sit in a row and blink as the motor steps
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: 'ULN2003' printed on the black IC in the middle of the board; silkscreen labels 'IN1' through 'IN4' and '+' / '-' near the header pins; a small white or blue 5-pin socket on one edge for the motor cable
easily_confused_with: L293D or L298N motor driver boards (different chip shape and pinout, meant for DC or bipolar stepper motors)
generic 16-pin DIP breakout boards for unrelated logic chips

example_connections.uno_pin: Digital pin 7 (example wiring from a DigiKey maker tutorial)
5V (or an external 5-12V supply for full torque)

required_extra_parts: external 5-12V power supply recommended for full torque instead of the Arduino's own 5V pin
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: Stepper.h (built into the Arduino IDE) or AccelStepper (third-party, gives smoother acceleration control)

hazards: low voltage overall (5-12V), minimal shock risk
the board and chip can get warm during stalled or continuous full-current operation
handling_notes: the motor's 5-pin connector is keyed and only fits the socket one way; don't force it
do not exceed about 12V on the '+' terminal; the board's traces are sized for small hobby motors, not larger industrial steppers
common_mistakes: wiring IN1-IN4 in the wrong order, which makes the motor jitter or spin the wrong way
powering the board only from the Arduino's onboard 5V pin while other parts also draw current, causing brownouts and skipped steps
mistaking this for an L293D/L298N DC motor driver board, which has a different pin layout and purpose

symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: a coil wire is loose or the IN1-IN4 order doesn't match the code's step sequence
symptoms_and_causes.check: reseat the 5-pin motor connector fully and confirm the wiring order matches what the library expects

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: no movement at all and the LEDs never light
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: no power reaching the '+' and '-' pins, or the sketch isn't running
symptoms_and_causes.check: measure DC voltage between '+' and '-' with a multimeter; it should read close to the supply voltage (5-12V)

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: motor is weak or skips steps under load
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: insufficient current from the Arduino's onboard 5V regulator
symptoms_and_causes.check: power the board's '+' pin from a separate 5V supply instead, and confirm the two grounds are still tied together

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With power connected, set the multimeter to DC voltage and measure between '+' and '-'; expect a reading close to the supply voltage. To confirm an IN pin is toggling, measure DC voltage from that IN pin to GND while the motor is stepping; it should switch between roughly 0V and 5V.

typical_suppliers: LCSC (bare IC only, not the assembled board)

confidence.notes: ELEGOO's own blog tutorial (elegoo.com/blogs/arduino-projects/elegoo-uln2003-stepper-motors-and-motor-driver-boards-tutorial) returned HTTP 403, and their wiki pages for this kit item returned 404, so board identity and wiring are confirmed from generic driver-board retailer listings (RobotPiShop, JLCPCB) plus the Toshiba manufacturer page for the underlying chip, rather than from ELEGOO's own documentation. Toshiba's own ULN2003APG part is listed end-of-life with TBD62003APG suggested as a replacement; this does not affect kit availability since boards are commonly built with whichever ULN2003-family chip (from Toshiba, ST, UTC, etc.) is in stock.
